detailed_rationale:
Aarti Drugs is a bulk-drug/API manufacturer (part of the Aarti group, sister company to Aarti Industries) supplying pharmaceutical intermediates and APIs domestically and for export. The business sits in the commoditized, cyclical end of the pharma value chain, and the numbers show it: 3-year revenue CAGR is -1.9% and quality score is a modest 31.4, reflecting the 2022-2025 API pricing correction that followed post-COVID capacity overbuild across Indian and Chinese producers. FY26 (year to Mar-2026) sales came in at Rs.2,565 Cr with net profit of Rs.195 Cr (OPM 12%), and the quarterly cadence shows a bottoming pattern: Q2 FY26 OPM 13%, Q3 FY26 OPM 9% (with an Other Income spike to Rs.12 Cr vs a typical Rs.1 Cr), Q4 FY26 OPM 13% (helped by an unusually low ~40% effective tax benefit that quarter -- a real one-off inflating that print), and then Q1 FY27 (Jun-2026) at Rs.703.6 Cr sales / Rs.50.1 Cr profit / 14% OPM, the best margin quarter shown. Stripping the Q3 other-income bump and the Q4 tax benefit, the underlying trend is a genuine, if modest, operating recovery rather than a one-off.

Balance sheet is unremarkable-but-fine for the sector: D/E 0.37, interest coverage ~9x, promoter holding 54.4% (down slightly q/q, not alarming). Governance-wise, GPCB revoked its closure order on the Saykha plant in July 2026 (environmental compliance matter resolved, ~Rs.10 lakh charge), and there is a leadership transition (new Chairman/MD effective Oct-2026) that reads as ordinary succession planning rather than a red flag.

Reverse-DCF: at a P/E of ~19-20x, the market is pricing a modest-growth, cyclical-recovery API business -- not a re-rating story. Given ROE of just 13% and a 3-year growth score in single digits, that multiple is fair, not cheap, despite the CSV's value score of 80 (which is anchored on trough trailing earnings). This is a fairly-priced, quality-improving cyclical, not a value trap and not a re-rating candidate.
recommendation_rationale: The quant call is Hold and the fundamentals support it: balance sheet is sound, margins are recovering off a cyclical trough (Q1 FY27 OPM the best in the recent series), and the valuation (~19-20x) is fair rather than demanding. There is no basis to escalate toward Sell -- the business is stabilizing, not deteriorating -- and no basis to argue for anything better than Hold given the still-modest growth and quality scores.
summary: Aarti Drugs is a bulk-drug/API manufacturer coming off a multi-year industry pricing correction. FY26 revenue was Rs.2,565 Cr with a 12% operating margin, and the most recent quarter (Jun-2026) showed the best margin in over a year (14%), suggesting the cyclical downturn in API pricing is bottoming out. The balance sheet is sound (moderate debt, ~9x interest cover) and the stock trades at a fair, not expensive, ~19-20x earnings. We see this as a stable holding rather than a name to exit or add aggressively.
positive_para: Margins are recovering: OPM has moved from a high-single-digit trough to 13-14% over the last two quarters, promoter holding is stable at over 54%, leverage is modest (D/E 0.37, interest cover ~9x), and a legacy environmental compliance overhang (Saykha plant closure order) was resolved in July 2026. The API/bulk-drug pricing cycle that hurt the whole sector since 2022 appears to be normalizing.
negative_para: Three-year revenue CAGR is still negative (-1.9%), and this is a commoditized, competitively intense segment of the pharma value chain with limited pricing power and full exposure to Chinese intermediate-manufacturer competition. Q4 FY26's profit was flattered by an unusually low tax rate and Q3's by an other-income spike -- normalize for both and the recovery, while real, is more modest than the reported profit trajectory implies. This is not a business with a visible path to double-digit structural growth from here.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~19-20x earnings, the market is pricing a stabilizing, low-teens-ROE cyclical API business -- consistent with what the company can plausibly deliver (high-single-digit growth as pricing normalizes), not a re-rating. Fair value, not cheap, not rich.
